summary:
Dusty Footprints: A Museum of Moon & Mars Machines is an interactive virtual museum about 10 NASA machines left behind on the Moon and Mars, from Apollo-era hardware to rovers, landers, and the Ingenuity helicopter. Visitors filter between All worlds, the Moon, and Mars, then open a card to read a first-person diary written as if the machine were talking to a student. Each card also explains how the machine worked, summarizes the real NASA science it made possible, and defines hard words in plain language, with NASA photos and source links.
It answers the challenge by turning dense mission data into a story for school-age space fans, ages 9 to 13. Facts come from NASA sources linked on every card, and the diaries are built only on those facts, so the storytelling stays accurate.
It matters because young people mostly hear about active missions. These silent machines paved the way for today’s exploration, and giving them a voice helps kids feel a personal connection to the science behind them.
details:
What it does and how it works: Dusty Footprints is an interactive virtual museum about 10 NASA machines left on the Moon and Mars, from the Apollo 11 Eagle descent stage to the Ingenuity helicopter. Visitors filter between All worlds, the Moon, and Mars, then open a card to read a first-person diary written as if the machine were talking to a student. Each card also has a “How it worked” line, a summary of the real NASA science the machine made possible, quick facts, and a link to its NASA source page. Hard words are explained in plain language, and seven cards have NASA photos with credits.

Benefits and intended impact: Students mostly hear about active missions. This project gives the older machines a voice, so young people can feel a personal connection to the engineering and science behind today’s exploration. It is free, runs in any browser, and needs no sign-in.

Tools and languages: Python and the Streamlit library for the website, JSON files for the content (objects.json for the machines, glossary.json for the definitions), VS Code for editing, GitHub for the code, and Streamlit Community Cloud for hosting. Facts come from NASA’s Space Science Data Coordinated Archive (NSSDCA) and NASA Science mission pages. I used Claude (Sonnett 5.5), an AI assistant, to help write code and draft the diary text from the NASA facts. And Chatgpt(Gpt-6) an AI assistant to help me brainstorm the project title and file name.

Creativity: The museum idea lets each machine speak for itself. The app also detects hard words on each card and defines them automatically, and keeping the content in JSON means anyone can add a machine without touching the code.

Factors considered:


Audience: I wrote for ages 9 to 13, with short sentences and a glossary.
Accuracy: Every card links to its NASA source, and the diaries use only facts from those pages. Some coordinates are noted as less certain.
Accessibility: Large readable text, and every photo has a caption describing it.
Scope: I focused on the Moon and Mars to keep the story clear.
